On the demo tables above:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(b.title) AS known_titles
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id;
```
This returns joined_rows=4 and known_titles=3. COUNT receives either * for rows or an expression whose non-NULL values are counted, and returns an integer. It does not change the tables.

old: A countdown subtracts one each step in this example. Starting at four gives 4, 3, 2, 1, so after 2 comes 1. Stopping at 1 differs from including 0. A Set is a collection of distinct values; duplicates are counted only once. Set(countdown).count compared with countdown.count can reveal whether the array repeats a value. That check does not prove the order, so another check compares the whole array. Knowing what each check can tell you helps explain why both order and uniqueness matter.
new:
A countdown subtracts one each step in this example. Starting at four gives 4, 3, 2, 1, so after 2 comes 1. Stopping at 1 differs from including 0. A Set is a collection of distinct values; duplicates are counted only once. Set(countdown).count compared with countdown.count can reveal whether the array repeats a value. That check does not prove the order, so another check compares the whole array. Knowing what each check can tell you helps explain why both order and uniqueness matter.

```swift
let repeated = [3, 2, 2]
let unique = Set(repeated)
print(unique.count)
print(repeated.count)
```
This prints 2, then 3. Set receives the sequence and creates a set with one member per distinct value; the original array remains unchanged. No order of the set is promised.

new:
A set also uses braces, but its entries do not have key/value colons. `{"nature", "art", "nature"}` keeps only one nature entry. `len(tags)` counts distinct members. Sets do not supply ordered indexes, so do not use tags[0]. An empty set is `set()` because empty braces `{}` create a dictionary. Choose a list when order and duplicates matter.

```python
tags = set(["nature", "art", "nature"])
print(len(tags))
print(len(set()))
```
This prints 2, then 0. set receives an iterable and returns its distinct values in a new set; with no argument it returns an empty set. The list input is not changed.

old: A timestamp records when something happened. JavaScript's `Date.now()` gives a timestamp measured in milliseconds since a fixed reference date. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second. To measure a duration, subtract the earlier timestamp from the later one. The result is elapsed time, not a clock reading. Both numbers must use the same unit and reference.
